Executive summary

SIGNAL-SUMMARY Delivery behavior is mixed and governance-heavy

The observed profile combines iterative team practices with approval, testing, and release controls that remain substantially stage-gated. The report separates that observation from any judgment about whether the operating model is appropriate.

Observed model Hybrid Iterative delivery + stage gates Empirical adaptation 78 / 100 Strongest dimension Release autonomy 42 / 100 Material constraint Accepted responses 42 / 45 93% response completion

Dimension detail

SIGNAL-DIMENSIONS Four representative dimensions

Empirical adaptation

Score78 / 100Coverage 97%

Teams report frequent inspection and adjustment of plans based on working increments and stakeholder feedback.

Limitation: this measures reported behavior, not causal effectiveness.

Release autonomy

Score42 / 100Coverage 92%

Release decisions depend on approval functions outside the delivery team and are commonly batched into scheduled windows.

Evidence: release approval, QA signoff, and deployment-window items.

Quality ownership

Score69 / 100Coverage 95%

Developers and QA share substantial quality responsibility, while final acceptance remains partially centralized.

Governance flexibility

Score38 / 100Coverage 91%

Scope and milestone changes often require formal approval outside the team, even when new evidence emerges during delivery.

Cross-dimension findings

SIGNAL-FINDINGS Patterns that emerge across dimensions

Claimed Scrum, observed hybrid execution

Observation
Teams report Scrum terminology and recurring ceremonies, while release, QA acceptance, and scope governance remain externally gated.
Implication
The operating model is better represented as iterative team delivery inside a stage-gated governance system than as a pure framework match.
Possible action
Map which gates are regulatory, contractual, risk-based, or historical before changing them.
Evidence needed
Gate purpose, lead-time contribution, exception rate, and change-failure data by release class.

Quality responsibility is shared, but final authority is not

Observation
Developers test their work and QA participates early, yet final release acceptance is still a downstream control.
Implication
Quality practices may be more integrated than the release governance model suggests.
Possible action
Test risk-tiered release authority rather than removing quality controls wholesale.
Evidence needed
Defect escape rate, rollback rate, approval wait time, and risk classification for candidate changes.
